But system design is really just this. You start with a product requirement, then figure out how to make it work reliably when the number of users gets huge. Let's build the mental model from scratch. Imagine a simple social app. A user opens it, loads their feed, likes a post, uploads a photo, sends a message. At first, you run everything on one server, one back end, one database, one machine. For a thousand users, that's completely fine. Then traffic grows, one server can't handle everything. So you scale horizontally. Instead of one back end server, you run several. But now users need somewhere to enter the system. That's the load balancer. It receives traffic and distributes requests across the healthy servers. But all those servers hit the same database and it becomes the bottleneck. So you reduce unnecessary reads at a cash like Redis. If the same profile gets requested 10,000 times, serve it for memory instead of querying the database every time. Reads keep growing. So you add read replicas. The primary handles rights replicas handle reads. Eventually even one database cluster isn't enough. So you partition the data, users in one range go to one database, others go elsewhere. That's sharding. Now files. You don't want profile pictures and videos inside your relational database. Put them in object storage like set three or R2. Then use a CDN to cache those files closer to users around the world. Now, someone uploads a video. Should the user wait while the back end processes thumbnails, notifications, analytics, and transcoding? No. So you introduce a queue. The request finishes quickly. And background workers process the slow jobs asynchronously. Next problem. What happens when one service crashes? One database goes down. One region disappears. This is where redundancy matters. Multiple servers replicated data, health checks, retries, failover. The system should expect parts to break. The goal isn't nothing ever fails. Its failure in one part doesn't destroy everything. Now add observability. Logs tell you what happened. Metrics tell you how the system is behaving. Tracing tells you how one request moved across services. Microservices, Kafka, Kubernetes, 10 databases. That's not good system design. Every component adds complexity. A cache can go stale. A queue can deliver twice. Replicas can lag. Sharding makes queries harder. Microservices introduce network failures. So you only add complexity when it solves a real bottleneck. That's the core of system design. Start simple, find the bottleneck. Introduce the smallest component that solves it. Repeat as the system grows.
